title: Who really is Jesus?
summary: Who Jesus of Nazareth really is: a historical figure and at the same time the eternal God, the Creator who became human to save me and reveal the Father - and who he wants to be for me personally.

sections.heading: The man who cannot be ignored

items.comment: Jesus himself asks the most important question: not "what do people say about me", but "who do you say that I am". Everything else depends on the answer to it.

questions.text: If Jesus asked you this question today, what would you honestly answer - and why?

items.label: "Messiah" and "Christ" mean the same thing (Matt 16:16)
items.content: Peter's confession "You are the Messiah" uses a word that in Hebrew is *masziach* and in Greek *christos* - both mean "the Anointed One". In Israel, kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil; the title pointed to the One who would unite all three roles. "Christ" is therefore not Jesus' surname, but a title: "the Anointed One, the promised Deliverer".

items.comment: Jesus is a historical figure - he was born in a specific place and time, registered in the census of a real empire. This is not a myth.

questions.text: What changes in how you perceive Jesus when you realize that he is not a legend, but a person from history?

items.label: Jesus anchored in history (Luke 2)
items.content: Luke deliberately sets the birth of Jesus within the realities of the Roman Empire: a census, the journey to Bethlehem, specific places. The Gospels do not begin with "once upon a time", but with dates, rulers and geography. This sets the Christian faith apart from myth: it rests on events in time and space whose setting can be checked.

items.comment: His neighbors knew his family and his trade. And yet his words and deeds burst the frame of "the carpenter's son" - people did not know what to think of him.

questions.text: Why was it hardest for the people who knew Jesus "from the ordinary side" to recognize who he is?

items.comment: Jesus does not say "I was, before Abraham was", but "I AM". He deliberately reaches for the name of God from Exod 3:14 - which is why his listeners want to stone him for blasphemy.

questions.text: Why did the word "I AM" provoke such a violent reaction? What did Jesus say about himself here?

items.label: "I AM" (John 8:58)
items.content: In John 8:58 Jesus uses the phrase *egō eimi* ("I am") where the past tense would grammatically fit. It is a deliberate allusion to the name of God from Exod 3:14 ("I AM WHO I AM"), in the wording of the Greek Septuagint. The reaction of his listeners (the attempt to stone him, v. 59) confirms that they understood it as a claim to equality with God - not a mere statement about his age.

questions.text: Why were these two words, for the first listeners, either blasphemy or revelation - with no third option?

items.comment: "In the beginning was the Word... and the Word was God." Before anything came to be, Jesus already was - and it was he who created.

questions.text: What does it mean that the One we meet in the Gospels existed "in the beginning", before everything?

items.label: "the Word" (Logos) as a bridge between worlds (John 1:1)
items.content: The term "Word" (Greek *logos*) carried weight for both cultures: for Jews it was the Word by which God creates (Gen 1; Ps 33:6), for Greeks it was the rational principle that orders the world. John joins both tracks and says something new: this Logos is a Person, is God, and became human. It is a model for speaking about Christ in language that different listeners can understand.

items.comment: The Word "became flesh". The eternal God did not stay far away - he came to dwell among us as a human being who could be touched.

questions.text: What does it say about God that he was willing to become one of us, rather than remain in unapproachable majesty?

items.label: "dwelt" means "pitched his tent" (John 1:14)
items.content: The Greek verb rendered as "dwelt among us" (*eskēnōsen*) literally means "pitched his tent". It is a clear echo of the tent of meeting in the Old Testament, over which God's glory rested (the Shekinah). John is saying, then: the glory that once filled the tabernacle has now "pitched its tent" in the human body of Jesus - God came to dwell among us not in a building, but in a Person.

items.label: "only begotten" (John 1:14; 3:16)
items.content: The Greek *monogenēs* means "unique, one of a kind", not "created first". Jesus is not "one of the children of God" in the same sense as believers: we become children of God by adoption (John 1:12), while he is the Son by his very nature. This distinction guards against thinking that Jesus is simply an outstanding man or a high angel.

items.comment: All things were created "through him and for him", and he "is before all things" and in him all things hold together. This is a description of the Creator, not of a creature.

questions.text: How does your relationship with Jesus change when you see in him the One "in whom all things have their existence"?

items.comment: The Son is "the radiance of the glory and the exact imprint of the very being" of God, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power - he is not a lesser being or a created angel.

questions.text: What does it mean that when we look at Jesus, we look at "the exact imprint of the very being" of God himself?

items.label: "the exact imprint of his being" like the stamp of a seal (Heb 1:3)
items.content: "The exact imprint of his being" is the Greek *charaktēr tēs hypostaseōs*. The word *charaktēr* meant a stamp and its precise impression - for example, the image on a coin. The picture says that the Son is the precise "imprint" of God himself: whoever sees Jesus sees a faithful image of the Father's nature, not an approximation or an inferior copy.

items.label: comparison block "the LORD of the OT = Jesus of the NT"
items.content: The New Testament repeatedly applies to Jesus what the Old Testament says about the LORD - this is one of the strongest arguments for his full deity. Pairs to compare on your own: - **Shepherd:** Ps 23:1 (the LORD as shepherd) versus John 10:11 (Jesus as the "good shepherd") - **First and Last:** Isa 44:6 versus Rev 1:17 - **I AM / the name of God:** Exod 3:14 versus John 8:58 - **Before him every knee will bow:** Isa 45:23 versus Phil 2:10 - **Calling on the name of the Lord for salvation:** Joel 2:32 versus Rom 10:13 - **The pierced one, on whom they will look:** Zech 12:10 versus John 19:37

questions.text: Which of these pairs speaks to you most strongly - and why does it matter that the NT "transfers" to Jesus the name and glory of the LORD?

sections.heading: God who receives worship and reveals the Father

items.comment: "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus - he is the face of the Father.

questions.text: What picture of God emerges when you accept that God is exactly like Jesus of the Gospels?

items.comment: Thomas says to Jesus: "My Lord and my God" - and Jesus does not correct him, but accepts it and blesses his faith.

questions.text: If Jesus were not God, how should he have reacted to these words? What does it mean that he did not reject them?

items.label: Jesus receives worship due to God alone
items.content: The verb "to bow down, to worship" (Greek *proskyneō*) in the Bible belongs to God alone. That is why angels (Rev 22:8-9) and apostles (Acts 10:25-26) firmly refuse to receive it. Jesus, however, accepts worship (Matt 14:33; 28:9, 17; John 9:38). Given the consistent monotheism of the Bible, this single exception is a quiet but powerful witness that Jesus is God.

questions.text: What follows from the fact that the only exception to the rule "worship God alone" is, in the Gospels, Jesus?

items.comment: Jesus receives worship (the homage due to God alone) - unlike the angels or apostles, who firmly refused it (cf. Rev 22:8-9; Acts 10:25-26).

questions.text: Why does it matter that Jesus allowed worship to be given to him, while his disciples and angels did not?

items.comment: The risen one calls himself "the First and the Last" - the title by which, in the OT, God the LORD described himself (Isa 44:6). And he adds: "I was dead, and behold I am alive".

questions.text: What does it give you to know that the One who calls himself "the First and the Last" also passed through death - your road?

items.comment: Being "in the form of God", Jesus "emptied himself", taking the form of a servant, even to death on a cross. Deity and humility meet in one Person.

questions.text: What does it say about the character of God that his greatness is revealed in lowliness rather than in domination?

items.label: "emptied himself" (Phil 2:7)
items.content: The expression "emptied himself" is the Greek *ekenōsen* (hence the theological term *kenosis*). It does not mean that Jesus ceased to be God - but that he gave up his privileges and glory, taking on the limitations of human nature and the path of a servant, all the way to the cross. The greatness of God is revealed here not in domination, but in voluntary lowliness for our sake.

sections.heading: Who is he for me personally?

items.comment: To those who receive him, Jesus gives the right to become children of God. This is the move from knowing about him to a relationship with him.

questions.text: What is the difference between "knowing who Jesus is" and "receiving him" into your own life?

items.comment: Jesus came to give life "in abundance". He is not a giver of rules, but a giver of life.

questions.text: What do you most need today from Someone who promises "life in abundance"?

items.comment: The God who created the universe says to a weary person: "Come to me... and I will give you rest". Closeness, not distance.

questions.text: What would it mean to come to Jesus with the very thing that wearies or overwhelms you today?

application.text: Jesus is not just a great teacher or a figure from distant history. He is the eternal God - the Creator, the "I AM" - who out of love became human to find me and to show what the Father is truly like. Looking at Jesus, I look at the very heart of God. So the question is not only "who is he", but "who is he for me".
application.challenge: This week, read one Gospel in full (for example Mark - the shortest), with one question in the background: "What am I discovering about what God is like by looking at Jesus?". Write down three qualities of Jesus that you would want to be true of God - and tell him about it directly.
